To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) HPV 16/HPV 18 integration is a frequent finding in tonsillar carcinoma, (ii) p53 accumulation is a frequent finding among HPV‐positive HNSCC, (iii) p53 mutations in exons5–8 are rare in HPV‐positive HNSSC, (iv) HPV 16 integration and p53 overexpression are not correlated, (v) HPV 16 DNA integration and p53 mutations are independent risk factors for HNSCC

(i) HPV 16 integration occurs in a substantial fraction of head and neck tumors, including 67% of tonsillar carcinonas; (ii) HPV 16/HPV 18 DNA could not been detected in premalignant mucosa, suggesting that HPV‐induced tumorigenesis in head and neck is a multistep process; (iii) p16INK4a is overexpressed in all tumors with integrated HPV 16/17 DNA, and (iv

(i) a subset of HNSCC exhibits integration of HPV DNA and p53 overexpression in the absence of p53 mutations, (ii) HPV integration is more frequent in tonsillar carcinoma and (iii) HPV‐associated tumors are less likely to develop in tobacco‐ and alcohol‐users
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular mechanism of HPV‐induced carcinogenesis and its role in head and neck tumour development.
the frequency of HPV 16 in HNSCC and the relation between HPV positivity and p53 mutation status in these tumors.
a novel subset of HPV‐positive HNSCC that exhibits p53 accumulation but lacks p53 mutations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HPV‐positive head and neck carcinomas exhibit accumulation of p53 protein, but not p53 mutation, and are not related to the well‐established risk factors tobacco and alcohol.
HPV‐positive head and neck carcinomas are characterized by a high frequency of p53 protein accumulation, but a low frequency of mutations in the exons 5‐8 region of the p53 gene.
HPV 16/17 DNA integration is present in a subset of HNSCC and is associated with accumulation of p53, but not necessarily with p53 mutations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in a substantial fraction of head and neck tumors (20–30%), HPV‐DNA can be detected by FISH and p16INK4 overexpression is observed.
the presence of HPV in tonsillar HNSCC correlates significantly with the absence of tobacco use, whereas HPV is not detectable in premalignant mucosa.
the presence of HPV in HNSCC is associated with the absence of p53 mutations, which is in contrast to HPV‐negative HNSCC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of HPV 16 in head and neck tumors is a rare event.
the presence of HPV 16 DNA in HNSCC is not associated with p53 mutations, which is consistent with the notion that HPV‐induced tumorigenesis does not depend on the p53 mutation status.
HPV is an independent risk factor in the development of HNSCC and that p53 mutations in these HPV‐positive tumors do not occur in the region analyzed (exons 5–7).
